_comment: Task Manager Plus - #500 known-problem-driver list. Seeded into AppPaths.SettingsDirectory on first run; edit the copy there (not this embedded file) to add/update entries without a rebuild - KnownProblemDriverService only re-seeds when that file is missing. Each entry is a quick flag, not a verdict: a file-name (optionally version-ranged) match is circumstantial evidence worth a manual check, not proof this machine is hitting the referenced issue. MinVersion/MaxVersion are inclusive dotted-version bounds; leave both null to flag the file name at any version.

drivers.description: SCSI Pass Through Direct (DAEMON Tools/Alcohol 120% virtual CD/DVD filter). Long discontinued by its own vendor after a well-documented history of boot failures and crashes when mixed with other storage filters or after an incomplete uninstall; modern virtual-drive software has moved to other drivers (e.g. dtsoftbus01.sys) specifically to avoid it.

Dell firmware-update utility driver with a publicly disclosed local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2021-21551); Dell shipped an updated driver and recommends removing this one. Presence alone is a leftover-install signal, not evidence of active exploitation.

Gigabyte platform-tuning utility driver with a publicly disclosed arbitrary read/write vulnerability (CVE-2018-19320) later addressed by Gigabyte in newer tooling. Frequently flagged by Microsoft's own vulnerable-driver blocklist guidance.

MSI Afterburner / RivaTuner Statistics Server kernel I/O driver with a publicly disclosed privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2019-16098); commonly cited in Microsoft's recommended vulnerable-driver blocklist. Widely installed and usually harmless in normal use - worth a manual check for an up-to-date version, not a sign of active compromise.

Intel Network Adapter Diagnostic Driver, part of several publicly reported "bring your own vulnerable driver" advisories used to gain kernel read/write access; also called out in Microsoft's recommended vulnerable-driver blocklist. Present on some systems from Intel diagnostic tooling that installed it but no longer needs it running.

Older AMD/ATI display kernel-mode driver, historically one of the most commonly reported faulting modules in Timeout Detection and Recovery (TDR)/display-driver-crash bugchecks on older AMD GPU generations. Modern AMD drivers use different module names (amdkmdag.sys) - seeing this loaded suggests an old driver package worth updating.

SpeedFan's kernel-mode hardware-access driver. Grants broad direct I/O port access and has a long history of forum-reported crashes/instability on newer chipsets it was never updated to fully support; largely superseded by other sensor-monitoring approaches (including this app's own LibreHardwareMonitor-based sensor reading).

Older Intel Wi-Fi adapter driver generation widely reported in community/forum bugcheck threads (STOP codes such as 0x9F and 0x133) on several Windows 10/11 feature updates before Intel shipped fixed builds. Worth checking Windows Update / Intel's driver page for a newer version if this is currently loaded.
Same family and history as netwtw04.sys above, for a later Intel Wi-Fi chipset generation - worth checking for a newer driver build if loaded.

Riot Vanguard anti-cheat kernel driver. Has a documented history of refusing to coexist with certain other kernel-mode drivers and virtualization-based security configurations, occasionally producing boot failures until the conflicting software or setting is changed. Expected to be present only while a Vanguard-protected game is installed.

BattlEye anti-cheat kernel driver. Occasionally implicated in compatibility reports with other security/virtualization drivers loaded on the same system; expected only while a BattlEye-protected game is installed - if no such game remains installed, this is a leftover worth investigating.

Older Oracle VirtualBox core driver generations had well-documented conflicts with Hyper-V-based Windows features (Device Guard, Core Isolation/Memory Integrity, WSL2) enabled on the same machine, sometimes preventing VirtualBox VMs from starting or triggering host instability. Recent VirtualBox versions use a Hyper-V-aware backend and don't have this issue - worth checking the installed version if conflicts are suspected.

Older Symantec/Norton real-time-protection minifilter. Legacy Symantec/Norton uninstalls have a long-reported history of leaving filter-driver registrations and services behind; if the corresponding product is no longer installed, this is worth checking for cleanup with the vendor's dedicated removal tool.

AVG self-protection minifilter. Community-reported cases of this remaining registered (and occasionally still attached to a volume) after AVG was uninstalled through means other than the vendor's own removal tool.

AMI firmware-flashing utility driver bundled with several motherboard vendors' BIOS-update tools, called out in multiple published vulnerable-driver advisories for granting broad low-level hardware access. Normally only needed transiently during a BIOS update - worth a manual check if seen loaded at other times.

An older CPU-Z kernel driver build reported in third-party vulnerable-driver roundups for insufficiently restricted I/O access; CPUID has shipped newer driver versions since. Widely installed and normally benign - worth checking for an updated CPU-Z version if flagged.
